assessment.nobel_worthiness: The optical lattice clock combines Katori's magic-wavelength idea with experimental realisation at fractional uncertainties near 1e-18. It turns an atomic-structure insight (Lamb-Dicke trapping with cancelled light shifts) into a new level of precision, allowing tests of relativity through gravitational redshift over millimetres, searches for variation of constants, and a basis for a redefinition of the second. This is atomic physics where theory and experiment agree precisely, and it is a field I know well.
assessment.attribution: Katori proposed the magic-wavelength lattice scheme (2001-2003) and demonstrated the strontium clock; Jun Ye's group at JILA drove the clock to its present performance and used it for many-body and relativistic measurements. Both names are in the credited list and support a clean two-person prize. Contributions of others (e.g. Takamoto, Ludlow, Hall and Hanzel on combs) are partly covered by earlier prizes.
assessment.maturity: Strong. Many independent groups (JILA, RIKEN/Tokyo, PTB, NIST, SYRTE, NPL and others) have built and compared lattice clocks over two decades, and international clock comparisons are routine. The 2005 prize covered the frequency comb and the 2012 prize covered ion-trap clocks, so timing is plausible now.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 2005 and 2012 prizes could be read by colleagues as precedent either for or against another clock prize.
Whether to also credit contributors such as Peter Zoller's early proposal work or the Ye-group comb-clock coupling is unresolved.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Cooling macroscopic mechanical oscillators to the quantum ground state and entangling or squeezing them is directly about where the quantum world ends and the classical one begins. It is not technology driven. Ground-state cooling, quantum-state transfer, and mechanical entanglement are conceptually clear results, and they connect to gravitational-wave detection and quantum transduction.
assessment.attribution: Cleland and Martinis demonstrated a quantum mechanical resonator in the ground state (2010); Teufel and colleagues cooled a micromechanical drum with microwave sideband cooling and later squeezed it; Aspelmeyer's group is central to optomechanical entanglement and cavity optomechanics. The credited three make a fair trio, though others such as Painter, Kippenberg, Harris and Regal also made decisive contributions, so the allocation of credit is contestable.
assessment.maturity: Good and growing. Several independent groups have reproduced ground-state cooling and entangled mechanical states. The field is arguably still developing, and the 2025 prize on circuit quantum effects touched neighbouring ground.
uncertainties: Many equally strong contributors (Painter, Kippenberg, Harris, Regal, Schwab) make the three-person limit difficult.
The 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum tunnelling in circuits may make the committee wary of a close follow-on.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Matter-wave interferometry with atoms gave the first atom-interferometric gravimeters, gyroscopes, and tests of the equivalence principle and measurements of the fine-structure constant. It is fundamental, using the wave nature of massive particles for precision metrology, and it has wide reach from geodesy to tests of general relativity.
assessment.attribution: Pritchard's group (first atom interferometers with nanofabricated gratings, 1991) and Bordé's theoretical scheme of Ramsey-Bordé interferometry are foundational; Kasevich with Chu demonstrated light-pulse gravimetry and later large-baseline interferometers. Chu already shared the 1997 prize, and Kasevich's work built on that, which complicates credit. The three credited names are a reasonable configuration, but not a settled one.
assessment.maturity: Mature in science and slowly maturing in applications. Several groups confirm sensitivity records and precise measurements of G and alpha, although some precision claims remain debated.
uncertainties: Partial overlap with the 1997 laser-cooling prize and 2001 condensate prize.
Different laureate subsets (Chu, Kasevich, Pritchard, Bordé, Mueller) remain defensible.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The Cirac-Zoller proposal for quantum gates with trapped ions and its experimental realisation made quantum logic a laboratory reality, and set the template for quantum computing hardware and for analogue and digital quantum simulation. It reveals new physics in the control of quantum many-body systems, and it is atomic physics at its best.
assessment.attribution: Cirac and Zoller supplied the 1995 proposal; Blatt's group in Innsbruck realised multi-qubit entanglement, teleportation and algorithms with trapped ions. Wineland and Haroche were recognised in 2012 for single-quantum-system control, which makes the incremental credit here a point to discuss. The credited trio supports a coherent configuration.
assessment.maturity: Strongly confirmed by many groups worldwide (Innsbruck, NIST, Oxford, Quantinuum, IonQ). Interpretation is stable. The question is whether it is already adequately recognised by the 2012 prize.
uncertainties: Overlap with Wineland's 2012 prize and with the 2022 prize on entanglement.
Whether the committee would prefer to reward the proposal alone (B035) rather than combine it with experiment.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Ultracold atoms in optical lattices realise the Hubbard model cleanly, with the superfluid to Mott insulator transition (Greiner 2002, building on Jaksch and Zoller 1998) and later single-site-resolved microscopy. It addresses many-body physics where theory can be tested against controlled experiment, and I find it a deep and unexpected bridge between atomic and condensed-matter physics.
assessment.attribution: Zoller (with Jaksch) gave the theory, Greiner and Bloch the experimental demonstration and the quantum gas microscope. Others such as Kasevich, Esslinger and Gross also contributed, and Zoller also appears in the trapped-ion entries. The trio is fair but not unique.
assessment.maturity: Well confirmed by many groups (Munich, Harvard, MPQ, ETH, Zurich and others). Quantum simulation is mature in its basic results, although quantitative claims beyond classical simulability are still evolving.
uncertainties: Zoller appears across several overlapping candidates, so the committee may need to avoid double-counting.
Overlap with the 2001 Bose-Einstein condensation prize.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The quantum spin Hall effect and topological insulators created a new classification of electronic phases, with protected edge and surface states and a clear link to Berry-phase concepts. It is a genuinely new organising principle and was experimentally confirmed. Its relationship to the 2016 topological phase prize is a point to weigh.
assessment.attribution: Kane and Mele made the decisive theoretical prediction (2005); Molenkamp's group observed the quantum spin Hall effect in HgTe (2007) following Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang. Bernevig, Zhang (deceased), Hasan and others are not on the credited list for this entry, so the configuration omits arguably decisive contributors.
assessment.maturity: Mature, with strong independent confirmation by ARPES, transport and many material families. Lasting impact is clear.
uncertainties: Competing claims between 3D and 2D topological insulator discoveries (Hasan, Moore, Fu) are not captured in this credited list.
Condensed matter is outside my primary expertise, so I defer partly to colleagues.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The experimental discovery of the Higgs boson completed the Standard Model and is a landmark measurement of the first order. The 2013 prize recognised the theory but not the experimental discovery. I treat this as clearly worthy in significance, but I defer to my particle-physics colleagues on how to weigh it.
assessment.attribution: Credit is complicated by the size of the ATLAS and CMS collaborations. Jenni, Della Negra and Virdee are founders and early leaders of the experiments, and Gianotti was spokesperson at the time of announcement. The Nobel statutes limit the number of laureates, so a fair person-based allocation is difficult, and the choice of these three is only one of several defensible ones.
assessment.maturity: Fully confirmed by two independent experiments and by subsequent coupling measurements. Recognition is arguably overdue.
uncertainties: Collaboration-scale credit cannot be fairly assigned to three individuals.
Whether to name Gianotti rather than one of the three founders is unresolved.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Squeezed states of light reduce quantum noise below the shot-noise limit. Caves proposed their use in interferometers, Kimble's group demonstrated squeezing, and Schnabel and others helped bring it into gravitational-wave detectors, where it is routinely used. It is a concrete display of quantum fluctuations that were once considered a fundamental limit.
assessment.attribution: Caves supplied the 1981 theoretical proposal and Kimble's group the early experimental demonstration (1986 with Slusher et al. at Bell Labs, which is a separate group). Schnabel and the GEO600 and LIGO collaborators made it practical. Slusher and Walls, among others, have a claim that the credited list does not include.
assessment.maturity: Mature in the sense that it is deployed in LIGO and Virgo and independently reproduced. The recognition value may be partly absorbed by the 2017 gravitational-wave prize.
uncertainties: Attribution is spread over a broad group, including Slusher, Wu, Walls and Vahlbruch, who are not all credited here.
The idea may be judged an enabling technique rather than a stand-alone discovery.
